item.stdout:
# Scale: how big a brain gets, and how fast it answers

Brain's row in every large-codebase comparison read **Unknown**, in both
columns, because nothing had measured it. This is that measurement, and the
command that produces it.

```sh
entire brain bench scale [path] [--json]
```

It reports index size on disk and query latency against a repository's size in
lines — the terms those comparisons are stated in — building the index in an
isolated store so it neither reads nor disturbs the brain you actually use.

**The headline is not flattering, and that is the point of publishing it.**

## Measured results

Apple M-series laptop, macOS, `syntax-only` profile, entire-graph
`v0.4.1-nightly.202609180615`, 8 fixed natural-language queries, 5 timed runs
each after one untimed warm-up. Every figure below came from running the command
above; nothing is estimated.

| Repository | kLOC | Files | Symbols | Index | KB / kLOC | Index vs source | Build | Throughput |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| entire-api | 174 | 746 | 12.6k | 40 MB | 237 | 585% | 7.2s | 24k lines/s |
| entire.io | 485 | 1,835 | 29.1k | 103 MB | 218 | 655% | 22.7s | 21k lines/s |
| entiredb | 628 | 2,596 | 35.9k | 112 MB | 183 | 536% | 25.6s | 25k lines/s |
| entire-brain | 746 | 1,777 | 50.3k | 193 MB | 265 | 363% | 19.8s | 38k lines/s |
| **kubernetes** | **4,786** | **15,921** | **325.1k** | **1,171 MB** | **251** | **654%** | **219s** | **22k lines/s** |

**Peak memory is withdrawn from this table rather than restated.** The figures
published here were read from `RUSAGE_SELF`, which never includes a child
process — and indexing runs in an external provider, so they measured the
harness rather than the work. Re-measured on entire-brain with the corrected
reading, the peak was **203 MB against the 70 MB this table used to report**,
2.8x higher. The other rows are wrong in the same direction by an unknown
factor, and restating them would mean re-running every repository, so the column
is gone until someone does. `brain bench scale --json` reports the corrected
`max_rss_bytes` today.

Code-search latency, against the semantic index:

| Repository | kLOC | p50 | p95 | p99 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| entire-api | 174 | 299 ms | 359 ms | 569 ms |
| entire.io | 485 | 1,329 ms | 1,701 ms | 1,777 ms |
| entiredb | 628 | 1,407 ms | 1,982 ms | 2,102 ms |
| entire-brain | 746 | 1,315 / 1,945 ms | 1,433 / 2,122 ms | 1,443 / 2,160 ms |
| **kubernetes** | **4,786** | **12,294 ms** | **13,031 ms** | **13,043 ms** |

The two figures for entire-brain are two separate runs of the same command on
the same commit, 48% apart. **Run-to-run variance at this scale is large**, so
read the order of magnitude and not the digits; the gap between 174k lines and
4.8M lines is far outside it.

## What this says

**Index size grows linearly with the codebase, at 183–265 KB per thousand
lines** — five to six times the size of the source it indexes. That ratio is
stable from 174k lines to 4.8M lines, which is the useful finding: there is no
sublinear behaviour to hope for.

**Query latency grows linearly too.** 299 ms at 174k lines, ~1.5 s at 746k,
**12.3 s at 4.8M**. Nothing flattens out.

Against the numbers competitors publish:

| | Corpus | Index | Search |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Augment (published) | 100M lines | 250 MB | sub-200 ms |
| Zoekt (published) | ~2 GB, multi-repo | — | sub-50 ms |
| **Entire Brain (measured)** | **4.8M lines** | **1,171 MB** | **12,294 ms p50** |

At 2.5 KB per thousand lines, Augment's published index is roughly **100x
smaller per line** than ours, and its published search is roughly **60x faster
than ours on a corpus 20x smaller**.

Carrying our measured per-line cost to 100M lines gives an index around **24 GB**
and a search around **four minutes**. That is not a tuning problem.

**So: Brain does not scale to a 100M-line codebase today, it scales linearly in
both dimensions, and 4.8M lines is where we have actually measured it.** That is
a worse answer than "Unknown" reads, and a far more useful one — it is a number
to move rather than a question nobody had asked.

Those competitor figures are their published claims, not something we ran. They
are not measured here and should not be treated as verified.

## What is and is not being measured

**`code_search` is the number that matters for this question.** It runs against
the semantic index, which is the store that grows with the codebase.

**`knowledge_*` is a different corpus.** Facts, history and docs grow with how
much a team records, not with how much code there is, so their latency says
nothing about codebase scale. The benchmark reports how many records that corpus
holds beside the timing, because a sub-millisecond number over an empty store is
not a latency for anything. The first draft of this benchmark measured only that
corpus, found 0.4 ms, and would have published it as a large-codebase search
figure.

**The corpus denominator excludes what is not the codebase**: `vendor/`,
`node_modules/`, `third_party/`, `testdata/`, and binary assets. Counting them
would inflate the denominator and make every ratio here look better.

**Latency excludes process start.** One untimed warm-up runs per query, so these
are steady-state figures for a live process, not `time entire brain search`.
There is no process-level cache between searches: repeated identical queries in
one process do not get faster, which is why the numbers track index size.

**It does not exclude the subprocesses a search spawns.** Every search resolves
its repository and checks index freshness through `git`, so each timed sample
pays for several process spawns — around 30-50 ms here, measured with
`rev-parse` at 10 ms, `branch --show-current` at 7 ms and the worktree-dirty
check at 14 ms. That is a real cost a caller pays and it belongs in the figure,
but it is not retrieval, and at the small end of this table it is a visible
share of the total rather than a rounding error.

## Reproducing it

```sh
git clone <repo> && cd <repo>
entire brain bench scale --json > result.json
```

The worktree must be clean — the indexer refuses uncommitted content — and the
repository must be a git repository, since the line count comes from
`git ls-files`. `bench scale <path>` measures a repository other than the one
you are standing in; the numbers in this document were taken with the form
above, from inside each repository.

`--repeats` changes the timed runs per query, `--query` replaces the query set,
and `--keep` leaves the isolated store behind for inspection.

## Limits of this measurement

- **One machine, and one run per row except entire-brain, which was run twice
  and differed by 48%.** Treat differences below about 2x between adjacent rows
  as noise. The 40x spread from entire-api to kubernetes is not.
- **The largest repository measured is kubernetes at 4.8M lines.** Nothing
  beyond that is measured. The 100M-line figures above are arithmetic on our
  measured per-line cost, offered as a bound on what today's architecture could
  do — not a prediction, and not a run.
- **`syntax-only` profile.** Richer profiles produce more relations and a larger
  index.
- **Languages the provider cannot parse contribute lines but no symbols**, which
  is why symbol counts do not track kLOC evenly across rows.
- The kubernetes measurement required re-initialising a shallow clone, because
  the provider emits an empty commit for shallow repositories and the indexer
  rejects the snapshot. The file content is unchanged; only the git history is.

# Scale: how big a brain gets, and how fast it answers

Brain's row in every large-codebase comparison read **Unknown**, in both
columns, because nothing had measured it. This is that measurement, and the
command that produces it.

entire brain bench scale [path] [--json]
```

It reports index size on disk and query latency against a repository's size in
lines — the terms those comparisons are stated in — building the index in an
isolated store so it neither reads nor disturbs the brain you actually use.

**The headline is not flattering, and that is the point of publishing it.**

## Measured results

Apple M-series laptop, macOS, `syntax-only` profile, entire-graph
`v0.4.1-nightly.202609180615`, 8 fixed natural-language queries, 5 timed runs
each after one untimed warm-up. Every figure below came from running the command
above; nothing is estimated.

| Repository | kLOC | Files | Symbols | Index | KB / kLOC | Index vs source | Build | Throughput |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| entire-api | 174 | 746 | 12.6k | 40 MB | 237 | 585% | 7.2s | 24k lines/s |
| entire.io | 485 | 1,835 | 29.1k | 103 MB | 218 | 655% | 22.7s | 21k lines/s |

name: test

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    # Release evidence is proved on the tag you actually ship from. Before
    # this, the repo had NO release-time evidence check at all: the gate ran
    # only on pushes to main, so a tag could be cut without its proof ever
    # being verified at the point it is published.
    tags: ["v*"]
  pull_request:
  # So anyone can ask "is the evidence release-ready?" without cutting a tag.
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6.0.2
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v6.4.0
        with: { go-version: "1.27.1" }
      - run: go vet ./...
      - name: Test browser controller request lifetimes
        run: node --test webui/tests/*.test.cjs
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v6.0.0
        with: { python-version: "3.14" }
      - run: python3 -m pip install coverage==7.16.1
      - run: python3 -B -m unittest discover -s tools/coverage -p 'test_*.py'
      - run: python3 -B -m unittest discover -s tools/release-hygiene -p 'test_*.py'
      # The adapters are only meaningful against the frameworks they adapt, so
      # CI installs them. Without them the suite still runs and skips those
      # cases, which would quietly assert nothing.
      - run: python3 -m pip install langchain-core==1.6.4 llama-index-core==0.14.25
      - run: python3 -B -m unittest discover -s sdk/python/tests -p 'test_*.py'

entire api — Make an authenticated request to an Entire API and print the response
Make an authenticated HTTP request to an Entire API and print the JSON response.

These endpoints are internal and can change shape without notice; where a
purpose-built command exists, its output is the stable interface.

The CLI attaches the right bearer token and dials the right host for the
chosen backend, so you don't have to plumb auth yourself:

  --to core   the control plane (default): orgs, repos, mirrors, clusters, /me
  --to cell   your home entire-api cell: /me/* activity, repo aggregates

Use --jurisdiction <slug> (e.g. us, eu) to reach a specific jurisdiction's
entire-api cell instead of your home one; it implies --to cell.

Both backends act as ENTIRE_TOKEN when set, else the selected login
(--context, else $ENTIRE_CONTEXT, else the active context), so a staging
login reaches staging's control plane and cells. The cell host comes from
environment's cluster listing; an explicit ENTIRE_API_BASE_URL names the
data host directly instead.

<path> is the full path on that host, e.g. /api/v1/clusters. These
placeholders are filled from the current repo's origin remote:
  {owner} {repo}   the GitHub owner / repo
  {repo_id}        the repo's Entire ULID (from its mirror) — cells key on this

The method is GET unless a field/body is given (then POST); override with -X.

When to use this:
LAST RESORT. Right in two cases: you are developing against Entire's own
APIs and want a raw response, or no first-class command covers your need.
Otherwise prefer the command built for the job (checkpoint, session, trail,
status, repo, …) — its output is stable, raw endpoints are not. If you are
reaching for this during ordinary work in a repo with Entire enabled, run
`entire agent-help` first; there is probably a command for it. When you do
need it, use this rather than hand-rolling curl — it attaches the right
bearer and dials the right host for you.

Examples:
entire api /api/v1/clusters
  entire api --to cell /api/v1/me/activity
  entire api --jurisdiction eu /api/v1/me/activity
  entire api --to cell "/api/v1/me/recap?repo={repo_id}"
  entire api -X POST /api/v1/projects -f name=demo

Current repo: gh/entireio/entire-brain  (auto-detected from origin; pass --repo only for a DIFFERENT repo)

Flags:
  -F, --field stringArray       add a typed parameter in key=value format; true/false/null/numbers are converted (repeatable)
  -H, --header stringArray      add a request header in key:value format (repeatable)
  -i, --include                 print the response status line and headers too
      --input string            file with the request body ("-" for stdin)
  -j, --jurisdiction string     target a specific jurisdiction's cell (e.g. us, eu) instead of your home cell; implies --to cell
  -X, --method string           HTTP method (default GET, or POST when a field/body is given)
  -f, --raw-field stringArray   add a string parameter in key=value format (repeatable)
      --to string               which backend to call: core or cell (default "core")

Who calls this / what does it call (targeted relations)

Usage:
  entire graph neighbors --symbol NAME|<file>:<line> --repo . [--relation CALLS] [--direction both|in|out] [--depth 1|2] [--limit 20]

Direct incoming/outgoing relations for one symbol, with definition locations, plus bounded two-hop paths at --depth 2. Use it when you want one specific relation/direction; for the full blast radius of a change, prefer impact.

Select a definition with --symbol <file>:<line>, or --symbol NAME plus --file/--line/--kind when a name is ambiguous. The ambiguity error prints the exact selector for each definition it found.

Flags:
  --symbol NAME|<file>:<line>
                             Symbol to inspect (required)
  --repo <path>              Repository (default: current repo)
  --file <path>              Disambiguate an ambiguous name by file
  --line <n>                 Disambiguate by line
  --kind <kind>              Disambiguate by symbol kind
  --relation <CALLS>         Relation family to follow (default: CALLS)
  --direction both|in|out    in = callers, out = callees (default: both)
  --depth 1|2                Hops to traverse (default: 1)
  --limit <n>                Max neighbors per direction (default: 20)
  --format json|text|agent   Output format
  --max-context-bytes <n>    Output byte budget for agent format (default: 16384)
  --internal-only            Drop unresolved external endpoints
  --exclude-tests            Drop test-only neighbors
  --head                     Query the committed tree (cached)
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                             Parsing depth (default: full)

Examples:
  entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol validateToken --relation CALLS --direction in
  entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol validateToken --direction out --depth 2
